column5: measured carpenter's work makes an idol
column6: The commentary's opening craft scene has measuring before cutting and shaping; Isaiah describes a carpenter stretching a line, marking, planing, and using a compass to form an idol, making a pointed contrast between measured human manufacture and the Lord who creates in 87:2–3.

column5: earth measured with a line
column6: The commentary links creation to an artisan's measured preparation; Job's creation challenge asks who fixed earth's measurements and stretched a line upon it, giving the image of measurement a concrete construction tool.

column5: God leads the blind and levels rough places
column6: The commentary joins straightening what is bent to the arrow point's guidance; Isaiah says YHWH leads the blind on an unknown road, makes darkness light, and levels rough places, combining the same two actions in a divine-guidance promise.

column5: YHWH goes before Israel to lead them
column6: The commentary says a staff is named as a guide because it precedes its bearer; Exodus pictures YHWH going before Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night to lead them, making the leading-ahead image a narrative act.

column5: Hebrew צלה and Arabic ṣ-l-y, roasting over fire
column6: The source commentary labels the Qur'anic word يَصْلَى with root ṣ-l-y and also gives a fire-working sense for straightening a stick; Exodus uses the related Hebrew roast verb for Passover meat cooked over fire, showing a cognate fire-use in its own ritual context.

column5: Hebrew עליון and Arabic al-aʿlā, the Most High
column6: The commentary's ayah calls God al-Aʿlā and notes that the same Arabic root names the highest game arrow; the psalm calls YHWH Most High over all the earth, so a related Semitic height term belongs to divine supremacy here, not a gaming share.

column5: every deed, including the hidden, brought to judgment
column6: The commentary says God knows what is public and hidden before describing the condemned person's fire; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including the hidden one, into judgment, joining hidden knowledge to accountability.

column5: Torah as plan consulted before creation
column6: The commentary reads creation as craft with planning before shaping; Genesis Rabbah compares a king consulting an architect's plan before building a palace with God consulting Torah before creating the world, supplying a Jewish interpretation of creation as planned workmanship.

column5: potter remakes a spoiled vessel
column6: The commentary's measure-and-shape sequence evokes preparing an object toward its finished form; Jeremiah watches a potter reshape a spoiled clay vessel as seemed good to him, a concrete craft scene that makes re-forming part of the maker's work.

column5: lots identify the cause of a calamity
column6: The commentary describes arrows drawing shares in a game; the sailors cast lots to discover whose account brought the storm, and the lot falls on Jonah, a distinct use of chance to identify responsibility rather than divide goods.

column5: Pur selects the date for Haman's plan
column6: The commentary's arrows distribute shares by a lottery; Haman casts Pur to select a date for destroying the Jews, showing a lot used to schedule a fateful act rather than allot portions.

column5: whispered words proclaimed from rooftops
column6: The commentary says God knows what is aloud and what is hidden; Jesus says what was spoken in the dark and whispered in inner rooms will be heard and proclaimed publicly, a specific speech-level counterpart that turns secrecy into disclosure.

column5: gaining the world at the cost of life
column6: The commentary says people prefer present life although the Hereafter is better and more enduring; Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and forfeit one's life, making the cost of that preference explicit.

column5: worldly good reversed after death
column6: The commentary contrasts preference for present life with the better lasting Hereafter; Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in his life while Lazarus received bad, but their conditions are reversed after death, a narrative counterpart to the choice's final share.

column5: measure of faith allotted to each
column6: The commentary's source gloss gives قدر the sense of setting a measure and each person's share; Paul says God has allotted each a measure of faith, a direct Christian example of individualized measure without claiming identical doctrine.

column5: fire tests each builder's work
column6: The commentary moves from craft preparation and fire used to straighten a staff to the condemned entering fire; Paul says the Day reveals each person's building work and fire tests it, shifting fire from the final punishment to an assay of workmanship.

column5: smith works iron over coals
column6: The commentary describes turning a stick over fire to straighten it and uses the same source-labeled Arabic root in 87:12's fire; Isaiah's smith works iron over coals and hammers it into shape, adding a concrete forge scene where fire serves manufacture.

column5: sons compared to arrows in a warrior's hand
column6: The commentary develops a shaped arrow and a quiver-like container; the psalm compares sons of youth to arrows in a warrior's hand, adding a family image in which the prepared arrow represents offspring ready for action.

column5: Hagar carries a skin of water into the wilderness
column6: The commentary develops how a leather waterbag is measured, fitted, treated, shaken, and worn; Genesis gives a concrete narrative use of a water skin carried with a child into the wilderness, where its capacity becomes life-critical.

column5: Israel as clay in the potter's hand
column6: The commentary's creation verbs are framed as a maker forming and ordering material; Jeremiah explicitly applies the potter-and-clay scene to YHWH and Israel, turning craft into a claim about the maker's authority over a people.

column5: fixed animal portions for the priest
column6: The commentary describes slaughtering a camel and sharing its pieces by game arrows, then contrasts that with a measured share from God; Deuteronomy assigns the priest the shoulder, cheeks, and stomach from an ox or sheep, a specific animal share fixed by law rather than chance.

column5: God gives growth after planting and watering
column6: The commentary glosses the Rab family as bringing something through stages toward completion; Paul distinguishes planting and watering from God's giving the growth, a compact image of development that culminates through divine action.

column5: builder saved through the fire
column6: The commentary's condemned person enters the great fire, while its craft scene uses fire to correct a stick; Paul says a builder's work may burn while the builder himself is saved, even as through fire, distinguishing tested work from final destruction.

column5: scripture is profitable for instruction
column6: The commentary presents the reminder conditionally in terms of benefit; Timothy says scripture is useful for teaching, correction, and training, making the ethical usefulness of instruction explicit in a Christian context.

column5: condemned sent to eternal fire
column6: The commentary's 87:11–12 moves from avoiding the reminder to entering the great fire; Matthew's judgment scene sends the accursed into eternal fire, a direct eschatological fire counterpart with its own judgment setting.

column5: this world as a vestibule before the world to come
column6: The commentary says people prefer this life although the Hereafter is better and more enduring; Avot calls this world a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation for the latter, giving the preference a Jewish ethical formulation.

column5: two ways, one of life and one of death
column6: The commentary contrasts the share chosen in present life with the better Hereafter and the fire awaiting the worst; the Didache opens by setting a way of life against a way of death, framing the moral choice as a path with opposed outcomes.

column5: Aramaic rabbi, teacher, and Arabic rabb
column6: The source commentary labels the ayah's رَبّ with root r-b-b and glosses a family of nurturing and completing senses; John's Greek text preserves the Aramaic address Rabbi and explains it as Teacher, a related Semitic authority term with a narrower use here.

column5: Hebrew שוה, making equal, and Arabic s-w-y
column6: The source commentary labels سوّى with root s-w-y and explains it as straightening what is crooked; Isaiah uses the related Hebrew verb in asking whom an idol can be made equal to, adding the sense of leveling or equality in a polemic against rival images.
